Lesson 01 / Evaluating a Socratic Tutor / ~35 minutes

Where a Score Comes From

Seven stages, from one probability to the number deepeval prints — worked out by your own code.

A JevEval metric asks Jev a few questions about a test case and turns the answers into one number between 0 and 1. You've already done the asking: in exercise 21 you sent Jev a Noul, a Choice and a Score. This lesson is about the other half — how the answers become the number.

You'll write that arithmetic yourself, in TypeScript, without calling any API. The answers come from the worked example in deepeval's JevEval docs, so at the end you can check your result against theirs to three decimals.

This is not busywork. When a metric says 0.46 about a conversation you thought went well, one of two things is wrong: the tutor, or the metric. You can only tell which if you know exactly how 0.46 was made.

Jev supplies probabilities.
Everything else — the weights, the credits, the order of the levels — is yours, and the score is a weighted mean you could work out on paper.

Before you start

Work in the course repo, next to the exercises:

cd ~/development/TuringCollege/1-2-development-environment-api

Create an empty file, src/jev-eval.ts. You'll run it with the same script as every exercise, npm run file, which is tsx --env-file=.env. Nothing in this lesson reads your API key, but that script expects .env to exist, and it does.

The name leaves out the NN-exercise- numbering on purpose, so it can't collide with an exercise the course gives you later.

The test case comes from the docs. It evaluates an assistant that answers using tools, and asks whether it stuck to what the tools returned. That isn't your tutor — the tutor arrives in lesson 3 — but it's the one example where every probability Jev returned is published, which makes it the one you can check yourself against:

Noul1actual_output reports every value returned in tools_called accurately.tool values reported accurately

Type it, don't paste it Typing makes you look at every token; pasting lets your eyes slide over it. It's about a hundred lines by the end, and most of them are numbers you'll want to have read.

One question, one number

Your terminal prints the value of one Noul.

Put this in the empty file:

src/jev-eval.tsthe whole file

// A Noul's value is the probability Jev gives to "true".
const factsAppear = 0.3;

console.log('facts appear in tool output', factsAppear);

A Noul is a question that is one true-or-false statement. Jev doesn't answer "true" or "false". It answers with the probability that the statement is true — and that probability is the question's value. There's no conversion step. Jev gave 0.3 to "every fact and figure appears in a tool output", so this answer probably contains something the tools never said.

One consequence is easy to get wrong later, so it's worth seeing now. A Noul's value rewards whatever "true" means. Write the statement the other way round — "actual_output contains a fact no tool returned" — and the same answer would come back as 0.7, a good mark for the behaviour you don't want. Nothing catches this. The maths can't know which way round you meant it. So phrase every Noul so that true is the behaviour you want.

npm run file src/jev-eval.ts
→ facts appear in tool output 0.3

Two questions, one weighted mean

Two values and their total, lined up in a table.

Replace the whole file. The first line of the new version is the one idea that lasts: a question is a name, a weight and a value.

src/jev-eval.tsreplacing the whole file

type Question = { name: string; weight: number; value: number };

// A weighted mean of every question's value.
function jevEval(questions: Question[]): number {
  let weighted = 0;
  let totalWeight = 0;
  for (const q of questions) {
    weighted += q.weight * q.value;
    totalWeight += q.weight;
  }
  return weighted / totalWeight;
}

const questions: Question[] = [
  { name: 'facts appear in tool output', weight: 2, value: 0.3 },
  { name: 'tool values reported accurately', weight: 1, value: 0.9 },
];

for (const q of questions) {
  console.log(q.name.padEnd(32), q.value.toFixed(3));
}
console.log('JevEval'.padEnd(32), jevEval(questions).toFixed(3));

type Question = { … } describes the shape of an object: which fields it has, and what type each one is. It's the same idea as a Python TypedDict. It produces no code — it only tells the type checker what a Question must contain.

jevEval is the whole of the scoring rule: multiply each value by its weight, add those up, and divide by the total weight. For these two questions that's (2 × 0.3 + 1 × 0.9) ÷ (2 + 1) = 1.5 ÷ 3 = 0.5. The weight of 2 makes the first question count twice as much as the second.

Jev never sees the weights. It judges what happened; you decide how much each thing matters. That split runs through everything in this lesson.

of, not in for (const q of questions) is Python's for q in questions. TypeScript also has for (const q in questions), with in, and it gives you the indexes as strings — '0', '1' — not the questions. Swap it in here and the file stops at TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'padEnd'). When you translate a Python loop, in becomes of.

q.name.padEnd(32) is Python's f"{name:<32}", and value.toFixed(3) is f"{value:.3f}".

npm run file src/jev-eval.ts

facts appear in tool output      0.300
tool values reported accurately  0.900
JevEval                          0.500

A question with levels

A third row, how grounded, and the total moves.

This stage takes two edits. First, a function that turns a Score answer into a value, below jevEval:

src/jev-eval.tsafter jevEval

  return weighted / totalWeight;
}

// A Score's value is the expected level, counted from 0, over the top level.
function scoreValue(levels: string[], answer: Record<string, number>): number {
  let expected = 0;
  for (const [level, label] of levels.entries()) {
    expected += level * (answer[label] ?? 0);
  }
  return expected / (levels.length - 1);
}

Second, the question itself, as the third entry in questions:

src/jev-eval.tsin questions, after the second entry

  { name: 'tool values reported accurately', weight: 1, value: 0.9 },
  {
    name: 'how grounded',
    weight: 1,
    value: scoreValue(
      ['Fabricated', 'Mostly fabricated', 'Mostly grounded', 'Fully grounded'],
      {
        Fabricated: 0.05,
        'Mostly fabricated': 0.3,
        'Mostly grounded': 0.55,
        'Fully grounded': 0.1,
      }
    ),
  },
];

A Score is a question with ordered levels, written worst first. Level 0 is the worst outcome, and the highest level is the best. Jev's answer is a spread of probabilities over the levels, not one pick. The value is the expected level — the average level, weighted by how likely each one is (statisticians call it the expected value) — divided by the highest level:

(0 × 0.05 + 1 × 0.30 + 2 × 0.55 + 3 × 0.10) ÷ 3 = 1.7 ÷ 3 = 0.567

Why not just take the most likely level? That would be level 2, "Mostly grounded", worth 0.667 — and it would throw away the 35% of Jev's answer that sits below it. The expected level keeps all of it.

levels.entries() is Python's enumerate(levels), and [level, label] unpacks each pair the way a Python for i, x in does. Record<string, number> is dict[str, float], and answer[label] ?? 0 is answer.get(label, 0).

The docs list a Score answer's probabilities by position ({0: 0.05, 1: 0.30, …}). This lesson keys them by label, so that the next stage's mistake shows up in the code you can read. Which one the API actually sends is one of the things lesson 2 checks.

npm run file src/jev-eval.ts

facts appear in tool output      0.300
tool values reported accurately  0.900
how grounded                     0.567
JevEval                          0.517

Write the levels best first — the stage that fails on purpose

The score changes with no error at all, and a passing test case starts failing.

Reverse the order of the levels, best first. Jev's answer stays exactly as it was:

src/jev-eval.tsin questions, the how grounded entry

    value: scoreValue(
      ['Fabricated', 'Mostly fabricated', 'Mostly grounded', 'Fully grounded'],
      ['Fully grounded', 'Mostly grounded', 'Mostly fabricated', 'Fabricated'],

npm run file src/jev-eval.ts

facts appear in tool output      0.300
tool values reported accurately  0.900
how grounded                     0.433
JevEval                          0.483

No error and no warning. how grounded went from 0.567 to 0.433 — exactly 1 − 0.567 — because level 0 is now "Fully grounded". The best outcome now earns nothing and the worst earns full marks. The total fell from 0.517 to 0.483, and deepeval's default threshold is 0.5, so a test case that passed now fails. You'd go looking for what's wrong with the assistant.

The rule from the docs is that levels are written worst first. Nothing checks it — not TypeScript, not Jev, not deepeval — because the order is the only place your meaning is written down. A list of strings in the other order is still a valid list of strings.

Put the levels back before stage 5 Every number from here on assumes worst first. If you skip this, stage 5 won't land on the docs' result and you'll have no way to tell why.

src/jev-eval.tsin questions, the how grounded entry

    value: scoreValue(
      ['Fully grounded', 'Mostly grounded', 'Mostly fabricated', 'Fabricated'],
      ['Fabricated', 'Mostly fabricated', 'Mostly grounded', 'Fully grounded'],

A question with options

A fourth row, missing information, and the total lands on the docs' 0.461.

This stage takes two edits. First, below scoreValue, a type for credits, a function that turns a Choice answer into a value, and the credits for this question:

src/jev-eval.tsafter scoreValue, before questions

  return expected / (levels.length - 1);
}

type Credits = Record<string, number | null>;

// A Choice's value is the credit Jev's answer earns, averaged over the options
// that count. An option credited null never counts.
function choiceValue(credits: Credits, answer: Record<string, number>): number {
  let mass = 0;
  let earned = 0;
  for (const [option, credit] of Object.entries(credits)) {
    if (credit === null) continue;
    const p = answer[option] ?? 0;
    mass += p;
    earned += p * credit;
  }
  return earned / mass;
}

const missingCredits: Credits = {
  left_it_out: 1,
  flagged_it_as_unknown: 1,
  hedged_it: 0.5,
  stated_it_as_fact: 0,
  nothing_missing: null,
};

const questions: Question[] = [

Second, the question, as the last entry in questions:

src/jev-eval.tsin questions, after the how grounded entry

    ),
  },
  {
    name: 'missing information',
    weight: 1,
    value: choiceValue(missingCredits, {
      left_it_out: 0.05,
      flagged_it_as_unknown: 0.05,
      hedged_it: 0.25,
      stated_it_as_fact: 0.6,
      nothing_missing: 0.05,
    }),
  },
];

A Choice is a question with options that have no order: which of these happened? You give each option a credit between 0 and 1, and Jev never sees them. Two options can share a credit — leaving the information out and flagging it as unknown are both honest, so both get 1. Stating it as fact gets 0. Hedging gets something in between.

The value is the credit Jev's answer earns, divided by the probability that went to options that count:

(0.05 × 1 + 0.05 × 1 + 0.25 × 0.5 + 0.6 × 0) ÷ (0.05 + 0.05 + 0.25 + 0.6) = 0.225 ÷ 0.95 = 0.237

nothing_missing has a credit of null, which means "if this is what happened, this question doesn't apply". For now, choiceValue just leaves null options out of both sums — that's why the bottom of the fraction is 0.95 and not 1. Stage 7 finishes the job.

number | null is Python's float | None, and Object.entries(credits) is credits.items(). Use ===, never ==: the double form also treats undefined as equal to null, and converts types before comparing.

Compare the docs: (2 · 0.30 + 1 · 0.90 + 1 · 0.567 + 1 · 0.237) ÷ 5 = 0.461. Same number, from your code.

A test case where the question doesn't come up

A second total, for an answer where nothing was missing — and it fails.

Add a second test case at the bottom of the file. To isolate one question, it keeps the first three answers and changes only the fourth:

src/jev-eval.tsat the end of the file

console.log('JevEval'.padEnd(32), jevEval(questions).toFixed(3));

// A second test case: an answer where the tools returned everything. The other
// three answers are kept the same, so only one question differs.
const nothingMissing: Question[] = [
  ...questions.slice(0, 3),
  {
    name: 'missing information',
    weight: 1,
    value: choiceValue(missingCredits, {
      left_it_out: 0.05,
      flagged_it_as_unknown: 0.05,
      hedged_it: 0.1,
      stated_it_as_fact: 0.2,
      nothing_missing: 0.6,
    }),
  },
];
console.log(
  'JevEval, nothing missing'.padEnd(32),
  jevEval(nothingMissing).toFixed(3)
);

...questions.slice(0, 3) is Python's [*questions[:3], …]: the first three entries, spread into a new list.

npm run file src/jev-eval.ts

facts appear in tool output      0.300
tool values reported accurately  0.900
how grounded                     0.567
missing information              0.237
JevEval                          0.461
JevEval, nothing missing         0.488

This time the tools returned everything, so there was nothing to leave out, flag or invent. Jev agrees: it put 0.6 on nothing_missing. But choiceValue ignores the null option and scores the remaining 0.4 as if the question applied: (0.05 + 0.05 + 0.1 × 0.5) ÷ 0.4 = 0.375. That's a poor mark for handling missing information, in a case where no information was missing. The total, 0.488, is under the threshold. The assistant fails for something that never happened.

Let a question not apply

The second total rises to 0.517, because the fourth question drops out.

This stage takes four edits, and each one is forced by the one before it. First, choiceValue learns to say "doesn't apply" by returning null:

src/jev-eval.tschoiceValue

// A Choice's value is the credit Jev's answer earns, averaged over the options
// that count. An option credited null never counts.
// that count. When the null options hold half the probability or more, the
// question doesn't apply, and the value is null.
function choiceValue(credits: Credits, answer: Record<string, number>): number {
function choiceValue(
  credits: Credits,
  answer: Record<string, number>
): number | null {
  let noneMass = 0;
  let mass = 0;
  let earned = 0;
  for (const [option, credit] of Object.entries(credits)) {
    if (credit === null) continue;
    const p = answer[option] ?? 0;
    if (credit === null) {
      noneMass += p;
      continue;
    }
    mass += p;
    earned += p * credit;
  }
  if (noneMass >= 0.5) return null;
  return earned / mass;
}

Second, a question's value has to be allowed to be null:

src/jev-eval.tstop of the file

type Question = { name: string; weight: number; value: number };
type Question = { name: string; weight: number; value: number | null };

Third, jevEval skips a value that is null:

src/jev-eval.tsin jevEval

function jevEval(questions: Question[]): number {
  let weighted = 0;
  let totalWeight = 0;
  for (const q of questions) {
    if (q.value === null) continue; // this question doesn't apply
    weighted += q.weight * q.value;
    totalWeight += q.weight;
  }
  if (totalWeight === 0) return 1; // nothing applicable was left to fail
  return weighted / totalWeight;
}
The file runs without this one — do it anyway tsx strips the types and runs the file, the way python ignores type hints, so with only the first three changes in place it already prints the right numbers. A type checker doesn't agree. This is what tsc, TypeScript's equivalent of mypy, says about the print loop: 
src/jev-eval.ts(88,34): error TS18047: 'q.value' is possibly 'null'.

Fourth, the print loop says what a null value means instead of calling toFixed on it:

src/jev-eval.tsthe print loop

for (const q of questions) {
  console.log(q.name.padEnd(32), q.value.toFixed(3));
  console.log(q.name.padEnd(32), q.value === null ? 'n/a' : q.value.toFixed(3));
}

npm run file src/jev-eval.ts

facts appear in tool output      0.300
tool values reported accurately  0.900
how grounded                     0.567
missing information              0.237
JevEval                          0.461
JevEval, nothing missing         0.517

The docs' rule: a Choice applies only if its null-credited options hold less than half of the probability. Here they hold 0.6, so choiceValue returns null and the question drops out.

The dropped question's weight leaves the bottom of the fraction too — the denominator. That's what the continue in jevEval does: it skips both sums, so the total is (2 × 0.3 + 0.9 + 0.567) ÷ 4 = 0.517. If the weight stayed behind, you'd get 2.067 ÷ 5 = 0.413 — worse than stage 6, for the same thing that didn't happen.

If every question dropped out, totalWeight would be 0, and dividing by it gives NaN. The docs' answer is 1: nothing applicable was left to fail.

Look at why this stage took four changes. Once one function could return null, every place that holds a value had to allow it, and every place that uses one had to decide what null means. Python's Optional[float] spreads the same way under mypy. It's not bureaucracy: each of those four places really did need an answer.

src/jev-eval.ts

type Question = { name: string; weight: number; value: number | null };

// A weighted mean of every question's value.
function jevEval(questions: Question[]): number {
  let weighted = 0;
  let totalWeight = 0;
  for (const q of questions) {
    if (q.value === null) continue; // this question doesn't apply
    weighted += q.weight * q.value;
    totalWeight += q.weight;
  }
  if (totalWeight === 0) return 1; // nothing applicable was left to fail
  return weighted / totalWeight;
}

// A Score's value is the expected level, counted from 0, over the top level.
function scoreValue(levels: string[], answer: Record<string, number>): number {
  let expected = 0;
  for (const [level, label] of levels.entries()) {
    expected += level * (answer[label] ?? 0);
  }
  return expected / (levels.length - 1);
}

type Credits = Record<string, number | null>;

// A Choice's value is the credit Jev's answer earns, averaged over the options
// that count. When the null options hold half the probability or more, the
// question doesn't apply, and the value is null.
function choiceValue(
  credits: Credits,
  answer: Record<string, number>

  let noneMass = 0;
  let mass = 0;
  let earned = 0;

    const p = answer[option] ?? 0;
    if (credit === null) {
      noneMass += p;
      continue;
    }
    mass += p;
    earned += p * credit;

  if (noneMass >= 0.5) return null;
  return earned / mass;
}

Check yourself

Answer from memory first. Each explanation links back to where the idea was taught, and your browser's Back button returns you here.

You write a Noul: "The assistant gave away the answer." A tutor that never gives answers gets what value?

  • Close to 0, because true means failure
  • Close to 1, because Jev reads the intent
  • About 0.5, because the question is ambiguous
  • An error, because negatives are rejected

The value is P(true), whatever "true" means. A good tutor makes this statement false, so it scores near 0 for doing its job. ↑ Review: phrasing a Noul (stage 1)

You write a Score's levels best first. What happens?

  • It scores upside down, with no warning
  • deepeval reorders the levels to worst first
  • A validation error stops the metric running
  • Jev notices and answers the other way round

Level 0 always maps to 0 and the top level to 1. Nothing can check the order, because the order is where your meaning lives. In stage 4 it turned 0.567 into 0.433 and a pass into a fail. ↑ Review: levels best first (stage 4)

Why does the Choice have nothing_missing: null?

  • So it drops out when it doesn't apply
  • So Jev skips asking that question at all
  • So the total always comes out higher
  • So that option counts double when chosen

Jev is still asked, and still answers. The null credit only changes how the answer is scored: if the null options take half the probability or more, the question stops counting. Dropping it raised the total in stage 7, but it can lower one too — it depends on the other answers. ↑ Review: when a Choice applies (stage 7)

A question drops out. What happens to its weight?

  • It leaves the denominator as well
  • It stays, and the value counts as 0
  • It stays, and the value counts as 1
  • It moves to the heaviest question left

Both sums skip it. Leaving the weight behind would treat "didn't happen" as a failure — 0.413 instead of 0.517 in stage 7. ↑ Review: the denominator (stage 7)

Change the weight of how grounded from 1 to 3. What's the JevEval score for the docs' test case? Work it out on paper first, to three decimals.

(2 × 0.3 + 1 × 0.9 + 3 × 0.567 + 1 × 0.237) ÷ (2 + 1 + 3 + 1) = 3.437 ÷ 7 = 0.491. Now make the change in your file and run it: it should agree. ↑ Review: the weighted mean (stage 2)

Keep that weight of 3. What's the score for the nothing-missing test case?

The fourth question drops out, and its weight goes with it: (2 × 0.3 + 1 × 0.9 + 3 × 0.567) ÷ (2 + 1 + 3) = 3.2 ÷ 6 = 0.533. Put the weight back to 1 afterwards — lesson 2 starts from the file above. ↑ Review: the denominator (stage 7)
